claims.text: There is a Pulumi blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' located at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ that covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, as described in the Pulumi AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK) in its early days, which allowed developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK supports only AWS, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers real-time debugging.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployment speed is slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers faster direct execution.
AWS CDK visibility is hard to trace errors, while Pulumi provides clear deployment state.
AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem, while Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports secrets management only through AWS Secrets Manager, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secret management.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, rather than generating an intermediary format.
Pulumi Insights (linked at https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for infrastructure deployments.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features, including custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi allows infrastructure to be defined in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C#, and deployed across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.

Pulumi Deployments (documented at https://www.pulumi.com/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/) enable more advanced deployment workflows including faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and more granular control over the deployment process.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose constructs are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform and potentially supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.

The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure through a single, consistent interface without having to juggle multiple tools or approaches.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
SST's team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode, while SST is still shipping.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework, from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications.
SST supports deploying to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define their app's infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST's docs page "What is SST" states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" states: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka's article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" states: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `package.json` for SST's platform package lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST's architecture, SST is responsible for reading `sst.config.ts` and resolving SST's own components, and for compiling components into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine is responsible for diffing desired vs. actual state, building a dependency graph, and ordering operations; Pulumi's Terraform bridge is responsible for translating each resource into cloud API calls; and SST is responsible for writing state to an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (self-hosted, not Pulumi Cloud).
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works the same way (embedded, no Pulumi account/Cloud required) for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The same provider bridge that lets SST use Terraform providers also lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Nitric's own docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Nitric's official providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang, which deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers, since SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket rather than in Pulumi's hosted service, and SST does not require a Pulumi account to work.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code; they work entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources that don't have a dedicated SST construct yet can still be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` package on npm is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week as of this writing.
npm download statistics for the `sst` package show 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5–11, 2026.
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now carries a larger following on GitHub than SST itself.
The GitHub star count for `anomalyco/opencode` was observed in September 2026.
SST's expanded team focus is a legitimate expansion of what the team works on, not a sign that SST is being abandoned, as evidenced by SST's continued releases and download numbers.

Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.

Pulumi's engine is embedded directly in the SST CLI, and SST keeps its own state in an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud, so no separate Pulumi install or Pulumi account is required to deploy an SST app.

SST's components are defined using Terraform providers, but those providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself, and SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.

Because SST's components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, users can define resources directly with Pulumi for anything that doesn't yet have a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
SST shipped v4.17.1 in July 2026 and the `sst` package continues to see roughly 796,000 weekly downloads on npm.
SST's broadened public attention to include opencode has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
The linked post "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK, told from SST's side.
The linked page "How Pulumi IaC Works" covers the engine mechanics referenced throughout this post.
The linked post "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi" describes the bridge that SST and others build on.
The linked Automation API documentation describes how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does.
The `platform/package.json` file cited is located in the `anomalyco/sst` GitHub repository, which was formerly named `sst/sst`.
SST's own team has publicly stated the architecture described (embedded Pulumi engine, Terraform-bridged providers, no Pulumi account) repeatedly since the Ion rewrite shipped.
